meta.title: Free 20-minute systems assessment | Gabriel Nadon
meta.description: Losing your days to double entry, spreadsheets and fragile software? In a 20-minute phone call, I’ll tell you what to automate first, what it costs and what it pays back. Quebec SMBs.
meta.ogDescription: In a 20-minute phone call: what to automate first, what it costs, what it pays back. Quebec SMBs.

jsonld.name: Systems and automation assessment
jsonld.serviceType: Operations assessment, automation and system rebuilds
jsonld.description: Free 20-minute assessment for SMBs: identify which manual tasks to automate first, the effort involved and the expected return.

hero.title: Your days disappear into tasks a machine would do <italic>without a single mistake.</italic>
hero.lead: Retyping the same data from one system to another. Keeping the “real” database in three Excel files. Holding your breath every time the old software glitches. In a 20-minute phone call, I’ll tell you what to fix first, what it costs and what it pays back — free, no obligation, whether we end up working together or not.

money.kicker: What a single manual task can cost
money.sub: recovered by a Quebec grocery store by eliminating the manual updating of its supplier prices.
money.plus: How much is yours costing you, without showing up anywhere?

signs.title: It isn’t “normal.” It’s just become invisible.
signs.prose: Each of these situations costs paid hours every week — and none of them shows up in your financial statements. That’s exactly what the assessment is for: making them visible, then putting a number on them.
items: Someone retypes into one system what another system already shows on screen.
Invoicing, payroll or orders take days — and an error slips through now and then.
Only one person “understands the system.” When they’re away, everything slows down.
You’ve already turned down a contract or a project because “the system can’t keep up.”
You know someone should “look into it,” but nobody has the time to stop and do it.

steps.title: 20 minutes on the phone — free
steps.text: You walk me through your operations and where things get stuck. I ask specific questions: how many hours, how many people, what risk. No preparation needed.

steps.title: You leave with an honest plan
steps.text: What to automate or rebuild first, the realistic effort, and the expected return. If it isn’t worth it, I’ll tell you during the call — and we leave it there.

steps.title: If we move ahead: in small phases
steps.text: Never a “big bang.” Each phase is delivered, used and paid back before we tackle the next one. You see the value in weeks, not years.

prices.quote: Clear prices, before the first call.
prices.body: You don’t have time to waste on vague quotes, and neither do I. Here are the real ballpark figures — the assessment is precisely what confirms which one applies to your situation, with numbers to back it up.

items.title: Assessment — 20 minutes
items.text: The call, the first ideas and the order of priority. Free, no obligation, no pushy follow-up.

items.title: Automation sprint
items.text: One painful process eliminated in 2 to 3 weeks: double entry, a manual report, data syncing. Fixed scope, fixed price.

items.title: System rebuild
items.text: The old software replaced piece by piece, in phases of about $6,000 — each one delivered, used and paid back before the next. Most complete rebuilds land between $12,000 and $30,000.

proof.label: In the field
proof.text: A Quebec grocery store eliminated the manual updating of its supplier prices — $56,000 a year recovered, without replacing its point-of-sale (POS) system, without downtime.

items.a: Perfect — this is exactly for you. You talk operations: orders, invoices, inventory, payroll. I translate that into a system, without jargon, and you stay in control of the decisions.
Great: they keep your servers and workstations running. I handle what’s nobody’s job — the processes between systems, where the hours get lost.

items.q: “We don’t have time for a project.”
items.a: That’s the symptom, not an objection: time is short because manual tasks eat it up. A sprint takes 2 to 3 hours of your team’s time in total — the rest is on me.

items.q: “What if it isn’t worth it for us?”
items.a: Then I’ll tell you during the call, in 20 minutes, and you owe me nothing. I only take on projects where the return can be demonstrated — that’s in my interest too.

contact.title: Twenty minutes. One plan. <italic>Zero commitment.</italic>
contact.lead: Tell me where your team loses the most time. I’ll reply within 24 hours with a few first ideas — or book your call directly in my calendar.
